title: Shia wedding card wording: samples
excerpt: What a Shia wedding card needs to carry — the Bismillah opening, both families' names, the nikah and walima details and the request for duas — with four sample wordings you can adapt: traditional, modern, walima-only and diaspora.

body.x: A wedding card has two jobs. The first is religious: it announces a nikah, an act of worship as well as a celebration, and asks the guests for their duas. The second is practical: it must tell people who is marrying whom, whose guest they are, and where to be at what time. Cards fail when one job crowds out the other — all poetry and no postcode, or all logistics and no soul. The samples below are starting points written for this guide, not official texts; every family's wording is its own, and the names, venues and dates in brackets are placeholders for yours. Adapt freely, then have a parent or elder read the final draft once before it goes to print.
The elements almost every card carries

The opening: Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim, at the head of the card
The hosts: the parents or family issuing the invitation, usually the bride's family for the nikah and the groom's for the walima
The couple: both names, each with their parentage — son of, daughter of — so guests from both sides can place them
The events: nikah date, time and venue; rukhsati where it is part of the same occasion; walima date and venue if held separately
The request for duas for the couple
The practical tail: RSVP name and number, and any note guests genuinely need

Two small disciplines save embarrassment. Give the date in both calendars where your guests live by both — the Gregorian date for diaries, the Hijri date because many families choose the day by it. And spell every name exactly as the family spells it, including the names of grandparents where they are named; a card is kept for years, and it is proofread by everyone who receives it.
Sample one: the traditional family card

For a full family celebration, with the nikah and rukhsati on one day:

Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim

With gratitude to Allah and the blessings of the Ahlul Bayt (as),
[Mr and Mrs ———] request the honour of your presence at the nikah ceremony of their beloved daughter
[Bride's full name]
with
[Groom's full name], son of [Mr and Mrs ———]

on [day, date, Hijri date] at [time], at [venue and address].
The rukhsati will follow the ceremony. Dinner will be served.

Your presence will honour us; your duas will bless them.
RSVP: [name and number]
Sample two: a shorter modern card

For couples who want the essentials carried lightly, often for a smaller nikah with a celebration later:

Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim

Together with their families,
[Bride's name] and [Groom's name]
invite you to their nikah

[Day, date] at [time]
[Venue and address]

Dinner and celebration to follow.
Please remember us in your duas.
RSVP: [name and number]

The modern card trades the formal parentage lines for brevity, which suits a couple hosting in their own names. If elders on either side would feel their place on the card matters — it usually does — the traditional sample's structure costs nothing and honours them.

The walima is the groom's family's feast, often held days after the nikah, and its card is issued by his parents:

Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim

With the grace of Allah,
[Mr and Mrs ———] joyfully invite you to the walima of their son
[Groom's full name]
and his wife
[Bride's full name], daughter of [Mr and Mrs ———]

on [day, date] at [time], at [venue and address].

Your duas for the couple's happiness are the gift we ask for.
RSVP: [name and number]

Note the one wording point that matters here: by the walima the couple are married, so she is named as his wife, not as a bride-to-be. Guests who missed the nikah also appreciate a single line — married on [nikah date] at [place] — which saves a hundred explanations at the door.
Sample four: a diaspora card with a bilingual flavour

For families whose guests live between languages, a card in English with one line of home in it is often the warmest compromise:

Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim

[Mr and Mrs ———] invite you with great happiness to the nikah of their daughter
[Bride's full name]
with
[Groom's full name], son of [Mr and Mrs ———]

on [day, date] at [time], at [venue and address].
Aap ki duaon ke talabgar hain — we ask for your prayers, and for the honour of your presence.
RSVP: [name and number]

The transliterated line above is Roman Urdu for "we are seekers of your duas"; a family from another background can substitute the equivalent in Arabic, Persian, Gujarati or their own language, or drop the line entirely. What carries across languages is the structure: gratitude first, names clearly, details completely, duas requested.
What you may adapt — and what to keep

Adapt almost everything: the order of the couple's names by whose card it is, the level of formality, the number of events on one card or separate cards for nikah and walima, verses or lines a family loves — quoted carefully and checked against a reliable source, never typed from memory. Keep three things in every version. Keep the Bismillah at the head; it is what makes the card a Shia wedding card and not merely an invitation. Keep the parentage lines unless the couple are hosting entirely themselves, because half your guests know the families before they know the couple. And keep the request for duas — it is the sentence guests remember, and the only line on the card still working for the couple years later, every time someone reads it and prays.
